item.title: Voice AI in vogue: Nvidia releases new open transcription model
item.abstract: Nvidia on Wednesday released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe , a free, open-weight model that transcribes audio in up to 40 languages. It also released version 2 of Granary, its open source speech dataset. Nvidia boasts that Nemotron 3.5 can translate 31 languages to and from English, handle recordings up to an hour long, and tell up to eight speakers apart. It claims to beat rivals on benchmarks, including Hugging Face’s Open ASR Leaderboard . These tools target developers building apps for business meetings and medical transcription, two of AI’s most established footholds in the workplace. Nvidia says developers can use the model, the updated Granary dataset, and tools like its NeMo Speech model to customize apps to recognize an industry’s jargon in each language. One drawback: Transcribe works with recorded audio, not livestreams. Still, the company promises Transcribe, at 30 billion parameters, can run on a single chip, from the Jetson AGX Thor robotics controller and DGX Spark chip powering new laptops , to Blackwell datacenter chips. It joins Nvidia’s open-weight voice models, including the super small yet powerful Parakeet (1.1 billion parameters). Nvidia’s latest voice entry comes during a busy period of AI voice releases: Mistral shipped Voxtral 3 earlier this month; ElevenLabs launched Realtime for instant speech in voice agents; and Salesforce released Launa-Omni, its voice model.

item.title: Survival LLM: AI assistant and emergency library that runs on your own computer
item.abstract:
An AI that still works when the internet doesn't. Survival LLM is a free AI assistant and emergency library that runs entirely on your own computer. Ask it how to keep food safe in a blackout, treat a burn, or purify water, and it answers from trusted sources and shows you exactly where each answer came from. Download for Mac 212 MB Download for Windows 25 MB Source code Free and open source. Set it up while you have internet; after that it needs none. What it does Works with no internet The AI model and the library live on your computer. Nothing you ask leaves it. Shows its sources Every answer lists the articles it read. Click one to read it yourself, with the exact passage highlighted. Made for emergencies Medical references, FEMA and CDC guidance, survival manuals, how-to guides, repair guides and about 930,000 Wikipedia articles. Pick your version The app is the same everywhere. When it opens, it checks your computer's memory and downloads the AI model that fits. More memory means a smarter model. Your computer AI model it uses Our emergency test Model download Mac with 128 GB or more memory NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super 21 of 22 right 80 GB Mac with 32–96 GB Qwen3.8 27B 21 of 22 right 18 GB Windows PC with 32 GB or more NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 19 of 22 right 25 GB Mac or PC with 16–31 GB IBM Granite 4.2 8B 14 of 22 right 6 GB "Right" means it got the main point of official guidance right on 22 blackout and first-aid questions, graded blind, in our tests on an earlier build of the library ( how we tested ). Smaller models make more mistakes, so the app always shows the source to check. Plus the library: a 9 GB download for everything (19 GB once installed), or 1.3 GB (3 GB installed) without Wikipedia and iFixit. Free disk space needed: the model's size plus 5 GB, plus about 27 GB while the full library installs (10 GB for the smaller one). Apple Silicon Macs (M1 or newer) with macOS 14 Sonoma or newer, and 64-bit Windows 10 or 11. Set it up in three steps Setup takes 20 minutes to about 2½ hours, depending on your computer and your internet speed. You only click for about 5 minutes; the rest is downloading. Download Survival LLM for Mac or Windows and unzip it. On Windows, right-click the zip and choose Extract All . Open it. On a Mac, double-click Survival LLM . On Windows, open the extracted folder and double-click Survival LLM.bat . Follow the setup. The app opens in its own window and downloads the AI engine (built into the Mac app), the AI model that fits your computer, and the library. Let it finish while you're online. The first time you open it, your computer warns you, because the app isn't sold through an app store. Mac: click Done , open System Settings > Privacy & Security , scroll down to "Survival LLM was blocked", click Open Anyway and confirm with your password. You only do this once. Windows: click More info , then Run anyway . What's in the library Plain-text copies of openly licensed (some for non-commercial use only) and public-domain references, searchable in a fraction of a second: About 930,000 of Wikipedia's most-read articles WikiMed medical encyclopedia MedlinePlus (U.S. National Library of Medicine) UK Medicines A to Z (public sector information) WikEM emergency medicine Ready.gov (FEMA) emergency guides CDC travelers' health U.S. military medicine and survival manuals Risk references for estimating micromorts: life tables and U.S. death rates wikiHow how-to guides iFixit repair guides Appropedia (appropriate technology) Q&A on home repair, cooking, gardening, the outdoors and ham radio (Stack Exchange) Each source keeps its own license, shown with every article; see the full list with licenses . Good to know It can be wrong AI models make mistakes, the small ones more often. Every answer shows the articles it used, so you can check. Private No account, no tracking. Your questions never leave your computer, and once set up it works with the internet off. Your own files Add PDFs, Word documents, ebooks and notes, like your generator's manual or your family's emergency plan, and the AI searches them too. They stay on your computer. Updates Check for updates, at the bottom of the app, installs a new version in one click and keeps your models, library and files. Battery On a MacBook Pro we measured about 100 W while it answers, for 5 to 40 seconds per question: a full battery answers roughly 100 to 300. A small generator or power station runs it easily. Update notes Already have it? Click Check for updates at the bottom of the app. 0.3.4 October 27, 2026 Reasoning setting: next to Send, choose how much the AI may think before it answers: Off, 1,000, 4,000 or 16,000 tokens, or no limit. At the limit its thinking stops and it answers from what it has, so a model stuck reasoning in circles still answers. It replaces "Think harder". When the AI looked things up but never wrote an answer, it now gets the best articles it found and tries once more, instead of showing nothing. Thanks to betsyisaac for finding this. Ask it to look something up and it searches the library, even if it first answered from memory. Answers say whether they came from memory, from articles it read, or from search results it didn't open. A warning when Reasoning or Length limit is set to no limit. 0.3.3 October 27, 2026 Mac: quitting with Cmd+Q now also stops the AI engine and frees the memory its model used. item.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
item.abstract: I’ve written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents —the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games . Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won’t pretend to be well versed in it—I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn’t think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... and it did . In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term —no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance. I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year. Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser. The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator . I used the regular Claude chat interface for this—it didn’t even need Claude Code. I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. I’ve found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent. This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all—I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here . Here’s the chat transcript that built it. It’s pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment. This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG: Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great Here’s that first version . It worked really well! I was inspired to increase my ambitions: Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way: Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good We’re back to prompts like “make it really good” here! Asking for a plot that “isn’t too cliche” seemed to work too—it’s a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story. Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems—things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location. Here’s that final game . It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through. There’s even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features. Once it was all working (and I’d iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I’m somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game—the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog—came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just “it’s a fantasy village and there’s a troll asleep in a cave”. Here’s the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game. I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here’s the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don’t think it plays nearly as well. This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week . It’s a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday ) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory. This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what “fun” is. The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn’t great to play. I prompted Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun” and then later to “Port this game to three.js” and the game was transformed. There’s a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up . Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of “mutators” that add variants of the rules. It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here’s a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna : Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5’s ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game . I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache ( screenshots here ), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work! I live in Half Moon Bay, California , home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival , which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition. I decided to try building a game that wasn’t just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season. I called it “Quarter Sun Cove”. I’m still iterating on this project, but it’s shaping up quite nicely.
